summaries.example: Imagine you have one ticket for one ride. In ordinary thinking, you might keep using the idea of a ticket without checking whether it is still available. Linear logic treats the ticket more like a resource: after you use it, it is gone. A rule may allow some resources to be copied or set aside, but only when they have a special mark.
summaries.summary: Linear logic is a kind of logic that treats formulas more like supplies than like permanent facts. A supply might be used once, combined with another supply, or saved for later. The usual rules called weakening and contraction are therefore restricted. Weakening normally lets us ignore a formula, while contraction lets us use it more than once. Special marks called exponentials can restore these freedoms for selected formulas. Linear logic grew from attempts to bring together useful features of classical logic, such as symmetry between statements and their opposites, with the constructive idea that a proof should show how something can be made. Because programs also use inputs, outputs, memory, and copies, this resource-based way of reasoning has become important in computer science.
key_ideas: Linear logic pays attention not only to whether a statement is true, but also to how its information is used.
Without special permission, a resource cannot simply be copied or thrown away.
The logic has different forms of “and” and “or” because combining resources can work in different ways.
Linear logic has been useful in computer science for describing programs, computation, and changing states.
summaries.why_it_matters: Linear logic gives people a careful language for talking about limited supplies and actions. It can help describe when information is consumed, when it may be copied, and how a computation changes a collection of resources. This makes it useful for studying programs, logic programming, concurrent systems, and other computer-science ideas.

important_terms.definition: A system for reasoning in which formulas can represent resources that have limits on how they may be used.
Something available for a task, such as a ticket, tool, or piece of information. In linear logic, a resource may be used only in allowed ways.
A rule that lets a formula be used more than once or ignored. Linear logic does not allow these rules everywhere.
A special mark that makes some formulas reusable or discardable, much like giving a resource a special permission.

questions_to_think_about: When should a piece of information be allowed to be used twice?
What is the difference between proving that something is true and showing how to build it?
Can a computer program be understood as using resources?
Would a game be fair if players could secretly copy every object they had?

summaries.example: Suppose a process has a single permission token for accessing a file. A linear implication can be read as a process that consumes an input resource and produces an output resource. If the process receives the token and produces a result, the original token is not automatically still available. By contrast, a formula marked with the “of-course” exponential may be weakened or contracted, so the corresponding assumption can be ignored or duplicated. The distinction models whether reuse is permitted rather than silently assumed.
summaries.summary: Linear logic is a resource-sensitive refinement of classical and intuitionistic logic. Its central change is proof-theoretic: weakening and contraction are not universally available. Thus an assumption cannot automatically be ignored or duplicated, and composing a resource-sensitive implication with its input consumes the relevant resources. This leads to separate additive and multiplicative versions of familiar connectives, representing different patterns of choice and combination. Linear logic also has an involutive negation, while preserving a constructive understanding of proofs. Exponential modalities restore controlled copying and discarding, allowing the system to express ordinary intuitionistic behavior and unbounded computation. The entry presents several perspectives: sequent calculi and focused proof search, graph-like proof nets, semantic models of provability and proofs, complexity results for fragments, and applications to programming languages, logic programming, concurrency, state change, and resource analysis. Some boundaries remain technically unsettled or vary among proposed systems, especially in extensions involving exponentials, units, additives, or non-commutativity.
key_ideas: Linear logic restricts weakening and contraction because formulas are interpreted as resources rather than unrestricted truth values.
Its multiplicative and additive connectives distinguish different ways of combining resources; these forms are not generally interchangeable.
The system retains an involutive negation and a strong constructive interpretation, linking classical symmetry with constructive proof ideas.
Exponentials allow controlled unbounded behavior, including reuse and discarding, and connect linear logic with intuitionistic and classical reasoning.
Proof theory, semantics, and complexity theory all study different aspects of linear logic, including provability, proofs as computations, and the cost of proof search.
In computer science, linear logic supports resource-aware types, logic programming, multiset rewriting, concurrency, and analyses of computation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Linear logic makes resource use explicit in a formal system. That is valuable when a program must track ownership, consumption, copying, or interaction rather than merely check whether a proposition is true. Its proof theory supplies ways to normalize and search for proofs; its semantics can interpret proofs as computational objects; and its fragments have been studied for their decision complexity. These ideas have influenced models of functional programs, logic-programming languages, concurrent processes, state-based systems, and analyses that restrict computation to classes such as polynomial time.

important_terms.definition: A refinement of classical and intuitionistic logic that treats formulas as resources and restricts unrestricted copying and discarding.
A logical rule that allows an assumption to be ignored. In linear logic it is not generally available for every formula.
A logical rule that allows one assumption to be used multiple times. Linear logic restricts it to specially marked formulas.
An expression showing that some formulas lead to another formula under resource-sensitive use; it can be read computationally as consuming inputs to produce an output.
Operators usually written ! and ?, which permit controlled forms of copying and discarding and recover expressive power associated with ordinary logics.
A framework in which a formula is associated with a proof, and a proof can be interpreted as having computational content such as a program.
A proof representation that removes some irrelevant ordering information from sequent-calculus derivations by using graph-like structures.
A proof-search method that separates choices that can safely be made from choices requiring coordination with the surrounding formulas.

questions_to_think_about: Does treating formulas as resources offer a better model of some computations than treating them simply as true or false?
Why might a proof system want to distinguish two forms of conjunction or disjunction?
How does restricting contraction affect the size or normalization of proofs?
Why are exponentials necessary for modeling behavior such as copying or iteration?
What information is lost, and what information is clarified, when a proof is represented as a proof net rather than as a sequence of rules?

summaries.example: Imagine a school has one lab pass. A rule says, “Give me a lab pass and I will give you a completed experiment.” In linear logic, using the rule and the pass produces the experiment, but the same pass is not automatically available afterward. A different kind of pass, marked as reusable, could be copied or ignored under special rules. This helps show why linear logic asks not only, “Is the rule true?” but also, “What happens to the resources used by the rule?”
summaries.summary: Linear logic is a refinement of two familiar traditions in logic. Classical logic is strongly associated with truth and symmetry, while intuitionistic logic emphasizes constructive proofs—proofs that provide a way to establish a result. Linear logic adds a third concern: formulas can act like resources. If a proof uses an assumption, that assumption may be consumed. It cannot automatically be copied by contraction or ignored by weakening. Once those rules are restricted, conjunction and disjunction split into additive and multiplicative forms. The additive forms are connected with alternatives or shared contexts; the multiplicative forms track how resources are divided and combined. Linear logic keeps a symmetric, involutive negation while retaining a constructive interpretation of proofs. Exponentials mark formulas for controlled copying and discarding. This resource perspective explains why the subject has become important in computer science, where programs manipulate data, permissions, states, and processes.
key_ideas: Classical logic emphasizes truth, while intuitionistic logic emphasizes constructive proof; linear logic adds careful attention to resource use.
Removing unrestricted weakening and contraction makes formulas behave differently from ordinary truth values.
Linear logic separates familiar connectives into additive and multiplicative versions, because choosing between resources differs from combining them.
Its special modalities, called exponentials, allow selected assumptions to be copied or discarded and help recover broader expressive power.
Computer scientists use linear logic to describe programs, state changes, proof search, concurrent activity, and resource-sensitive computation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many computer systems must track more than truth. They must record whether a file permission has been used, whether data may be duplicated, or how several processes share information. Linear logic offers formal tools for expressing these restrictions. Its proof systems can guide proof search, its proofs can correspond to computational objects, and its resource-sensitive formulas can help specify programs and concurrent systems. It also gives philosophers and logicians a way to compare classical and intuitionistic reasoning by showing exactly what changes when copying and discarding are no longer free.

important_terms.definition: A logic that studies statements while tracking whether their information or assumptions are used, saved, copied, or consumed.
An assumption or piece of information that is available for a proof or computation and may have limits on its use.
A rule that permits an assumption to be left unused. Linear logic restricts this rule rather than applying it automatically.
A rule that permits an assumption to be used repeatedly. Linear logic restricts this rule rather than applying it automatically.
A special operator, often written ! or ?, that gives selected formulas permission for controlled reuse or disposal.
A method of presenting proofs with collections of formulas on one or both sides of a turnstile; in linear logic, the number of repeated formulas matters.

questions_to_think_about: What could go wrong if a computer program were allowed to copy every resource without limit?
How is a choice between two tools different from receiving both tools together?
Why might a proof need to show not just that a conclusion follows, but how its assumptions were used?
When would it be helpful to treat the order or number of items in a collection as meaningful?
Should a logic that models computation permit every rule found in ordinary mathematics?
